title: Annotatio I §.II Schmidius: τὸ ῥητόν includes tropic acceptance — Matt. 16:16 and John 6:51 both literal; no Calvinist quarrel so far
pass_a_gloss: To whom Sebastian Schmidius also agrees, even as to application to the proposition of the Sacred Supper now in question — Treatise on the principles or Foundations of the presence of the body and Blood of Christ in the Sacred Supper, ch. 3, §. 17. The Literal sense, or τὸ ῥητόν, he says, is that sense which the words themselves immediately render, all circumstances considered: where we gladly admit that τὸ ῥητόν or the literal sense is not only what words taken properly can give, but also what they furnish when accepted tropically. So that that literal sense is suggested now by words accepted properly, now by words used tropically. Thus not only Peter’s words, Matt. 16:16, You are the Son of the living God, have a literal sense, but also the Lord Jesus’s own words, John 6:51, I am the living bread — though here there is a trope, there none. And thus far there will be no controversy between us and the Calvinists, p. 18 at the end & 19.
pass_b_english: Sebastian Schmidius agrees for the Supper proposition itself: the literal sense / τὸ ῥητόν is what the words immediately yield when all circumstances are weighed.
He gladly allows that τὸ ῥητόν covers not only words taken properly but also words taken tropically.

So Peter’s You are the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:16) and Christ’s I am the living bread (John 6:51) are both literal — though only the second is a trope — and thus far there is no quarrel with the Calvinists (pp. 18–19).
source_text: Cui adstipulatur, etiam quà applicationem ad propositionem S. Coenae de qua nunc quaeritur, Sebastian. Schmidius Tract. de principiis seu Fundamentis praesentiae corporis & Sanguinis Christi in S. Coena cap. 3. §. 17. Literalis sensus, seu τὸ ῥητόν, ait, est is sensus, quem verba ipsa immediatè, consideratis omnibus circumstantiis, reddunt: ubi libenter admittimus τὸ ῥητόν seu literalem sensum non tantùm esse, quem verba propriè sumta dare possunt, sed etiam quem tropicè accepta subministrant. Ut adeò literalem istum sensum, modò, verba propriè accepta, modò, verba tropicè usurpata, suggerant. Sic literalem sensum habent non tantum verba Petri, Matth. 16. vers. 16. Tu es Filius Dei viventis, sed & verba ipsius Domini Jesu, Joh. 6. vers. 51. Ego sum panis vivus; licet hic tropus sit, ibi nullus. Et hactenus inter nos & Calvinianos nihil erit controversiae, p. 18. in fin. & 19.
notes: Schmidius; tropic τὸ ῥητόν; Matt 16 / John 6:51.
